Estimate single, combined and interaction effects under null models

Source: R/estimate.R, R/external.R
estimate_interactions.Rd

Computes, for every identifiable contrast set of the design (see describe_design()), the effect of each stressor alone, the effect of their combination and its deviation from what each null model predicts. This is post-estimation inference: one model per response, one or more null models tested from its predictions with the same criteria (Madge Pimentel et al. 2025). The model is either the one selected by fit_responses() or one fitted outside must, such as stats::lm(), stats::glm(), mgcv::gam(), lme4::glmer() or glmmTMB::glmmTMB() (see "Models fitted outside must"). By default the null model is simple addition (see "Default null model").

Usage

estimate_interactions(fit, ...)

# S3 method for class 'must_fit'
estimate_interactions(
  fit,
  null_models = "AD",
  inference = "simulation",
  correction = "small_sample",
  n_sim = 10000L,
  level = 0.95,
  p_adjust = "BH",
  overall = TRUE,
  sensitivity = NULL,
  seed = NULL,
  sam_shape = 3.2,
  margin = NULL,
  ...
)

# Default S3 method
estimate_interactions(
  fit,
  design,
  null_models = "AD",
  inference = "simulation",
  correction = "small_sample",
  n_sim = 10000L,
  level = 0.95,
  p_adjust = "BH",
  overall = TRUE,
  sensitivity = FALSE,
  seed = NULL,
  sam_shape = 3.2,
  margin = NULL,
  df = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

fit

A must_fit object from fit_responses(), or a model fitted outside must whose predictors include the stressor columns of design (any model supported by the emmeans package).

...

For a model fitted outside must: further arguments passed to emmeans::ref_grid(), such as at (values of other numeric predictors), offset, lmer.df or component. Not used otherwise.

null_models

Null models to evaluate: any of "AD" (simple addition), "MU" (multiplicative), "DO" (dominance), "BL" (Bliss independence), "SAM" (stress addition model) and "CA" (concentration addition, or Loewe additivity). Default "AD", the null model that flagged the fewest false interactions across mechanisms in simulations (see "Default null model"); c("AD", "MU", "DO") gives the three null models of Madge Pimentel et al. (2025). It can also be the output of suggest_null_models(): its null models are estimated, and its criteria and reasons are kept in settings$null_model_choice.

inference

"simulation" (default; Krinsky–Robb: draws of the fixed effects from their estimated distribution) or "delta" (delta method; not for "DO").

correction

"small_sample" (default) or "none". For a must_fit with "small_sample", the covariance of the fixed effects comes from the REML refit of the selected model and the sampling distribution is a t with the degrees of freedom of the experimental units (see Details); for a model fitted outside must, a t with the degrees of freedom given by emmeans (residual ones for a glm with an estimated dispersion) or by df. "none" uses the normal distribution (and, for a must_fit, the maximum-likelihood covariance), as in Madge Pimentel et al. (2025); with few replicates its tests reject a true null model too often.

n_sim

Number of draws for inference = "simulation", and for the tests of combinations with only zeros with either inference. Default 10000.

level

Confidence level of the intervals. Default 0.95.

p_adjust

Method of stats::p.adjust() used across contrast sets and sampling times (see Details). Default "BH".

overall

If TRUE (default) and the design has two or more sampling times after any baseline, adds for each set the average of each effect over those times (time = "overall").

sensitivity

Whether an increase in the response means sensitivity (mortality, damage) rather than tolerance. For a must_fit: NULL (default) or the names of such responses; for a model fitted outside must: TRUE or FALSE (default). When the response is a proportion (trials in fit_responses(); a binomial-type family or a logit, probit, cloglog or cauchit link in a model fitted outside must), every null model is then applied to its complement (1 - p, e.g. survival instead of mortality); for other responses the MU, DO and BL rows are "not_applicable", because those null models assume that an increase means tolerance.

seed

NULL (default) or a whole number. The simulation runs with this seed through withr::with_seed(), which restores the random number state of the session afterwards. With NULL, a seed is drawn from the session's random number stream; either way it is stored in settings$seed, so the estimates can be repeated exactly.

sam_shape

Shape of the symmetric beta distribution of the stress capacity of individuals in the stress addition model (both of its parameters). Default 3.2, the value fitted by Liess et al. (2016).

margin

NULL (default) or a positive number: the equivalence margin for the relative deviation of each interaction (relative, a share of the response of the reference cell; 0.1 means 10%). With a margin, each interaction is also tested for equivalence (p_equivalence), and classify_interactions() and summary() give its verdict (see "Equivalence"). It has no default: what deviation is negligible is a scientific decision, to be declared before the analysis.

design

For a model fitted outside must: the output of describe_design() for the data the model was fitted to. Its stressors, control levels, time, by, baseline, max_order and background define the contrast sets.

df

For a model fitted outside must: NULL (default), for the degrees of freedom that emmeans gives for each contrast, or a single positive number used for every contrast (for example, experimental units minus treatment combinations). Only with correction = "small_sample". emmeans gives infinite degrees of freedom to a stats::glm() whose dispersion is estimated (quasi-Poisson, quasi-binomial and the other families except Poisson and binomial); with NULL, its residual degrees of freedom are used instead, as summary.glm() does. MASS::glm.nb() keeps the normal distribution, as in its summary.

data

For a model fitted outside must: the data it was fitted to, when emmeans cannot recover them from the model (for example, a mgcv::gam() whose formula transforms a column, as in factor(day)). Default NULL.

Value

An object of class must_interactions, a list with estimates, design, settings and diagnostics. estimates is a data frame with one row per response, contrast set, sampling time, null model and quantity, and columns:

  • response, context and the by columns, time (NA without time, "overall" for averages over times), set_id, order, stressors, levels, background (levels of the stressors held outside the set): what is estimated.

  • null_model ("AD", "MU", "DO", "BL", "SAM", "CA") and scale ("response", "log(response)" or "response / control"): what "no interaction" means and on which scale.

  • component: "single" (one stressor alone vs the reference cell; its name in stressor), "combined" (all stressors of the set vs the reference) or "interaction".

  • estimand for interactions: "net" (deviation of the combination from the null-model combination of the single effects) or "pure" (highest-order interaction once all lower-order ones are removed; only for three or more stressors; the emergent interaction under BL).

  • estimate, se (standard error; with inference = "simulation", the standard deviation of the simulated estimates before they are scaled to a t distribution, comparable with the delta method), lower, upper, level, df (degrees of freedom of the t distribution; Inf for the normal), p_value, p_adjusted, mc_se (Monte Carlo standard error of a simulated p-value).

  • observed and expected (interactions only, response scale): the fitted mean of the combination and the value the null model predicts.

  • relative, relative_lower and relative_upper (interactions only): the relative deviation (observed - expected) / reference, the same quantity for every null model, and its interval at level (see "Equivalence").

  • p_equivalence and p_equivalence_adjusted (interactions, with a margin only): p-value of the test of equivalence, raw and adjusted like p_adjusted.

  • rescaled and rescaled_class (BL interactions only): the interaction relative to its extremes and its descriptive class (see "Bliss independence").

  • inference, status ("ok", "boundary" (tested from the probability of a combination with only zeros, see Details), "not_estimable", "not_identifiable", "not_defined" or "not_applicable"), reason, note ("expected_below_zero" when simple addition predicts an impossible negative value for a non-negative response; "no_point_expectation" when dominance gives no single expected value; "reference_not_positive" when the relative deviation cannot be computed because the reference mean (or one of its draws) is not positive; "equivalence_not_tested" when the closest means at the margin could not be found (see "Equivalence"); "confounded_with_groups" for the sets flagged in sets$confounded by describe_design(); "complement" for responses analysed as 1 - p; several notes are separated by "; ").

settings holds the arguments used (with the seed and whether it was given), the versions of must and R (and emmeans, for a model fitted outside must), the criteria behind the null models when they came from suggest_null_models() and, for a must_fit, a summary of the models (fit): what report_interactions() describes.

For a model fitted outside must, diagnostics$means has the mean of every treatment combination (and time) that was used: its estimate and standard error on the link scale, the mean on the response scale, the degrees of freedom given by emmeans and, if it could not be used, why ("nonestimable", "no_se" or "boundary").

Details

With y0 the mean of the reference cell (the control, or the background combination of the other stressors), yi that of stressor i alone and yS that of the combination of the stressors in S:

Two stressors (Madge Pimentel et al. 2025, eqs. 1–3 and 7–9): $$AD:\ y_{AB} - y_A - y_B + y_0$$ $$MU:\ \ln y_{AB} - \ln y_A - \ln y_B + \ln y_0$$ $$DO:\ \min(y_{AB}, y_0) - \min(y_A, y_B)$$

k stressors. The net deviation compares the combination with the null-model combination of the single effects only: \(y_K - \sum_i y_i + (k-1) y_0\) (AD) or the same on the log scale (MU). The pure k-th order interaction is the inclusion–exclusion sum \(\sum_{S \subseteq K} (-1)^{k-|S|} f(y_S)\), with f the identity (AD) or the logarithm (MU). The net deviation equals the sum of the pure interactions of all subsets of K with two or more stressors: a non-additive net deviation is not, by itself, evidence of a k-way interaction. The dominance model is defined for two stressors only.

Single and combined effects are differences from the reference cell on the response scale (AD) or log ratios (MU). For DO only the interaction is reported; its single effects are those of AD.

Inference. "simulation" follows the Krinsky–Robb method used by Madge Pimentel et al. (2025): percentile intervals and two-sided p-values \(2 \min(P(x \le 0), P(x \ge 0))\) of the simulated estimates, bounded below by 1/n_sim. "delta" uses Wald tests; it is not valid for DO, which is not differentiable where the ranking of the means changes. Uncertainty from the selection of the error distribution is not included.

Small-sample correction. With few replicates, a normal distribution with the maximum-likelihood covariance understates the uncertainty: in simulated 2 x 2 Gaussian experiments with three replicates the AD test then rejected a true null model in about 13% of the experiments instead of 5%. With correction = "small_sample" the covariance comes from the REML refit and the draws come from a multivariate t (normal draws scaled by \(\sqrt{\nu / \chi^2_\nu}\)), whose degrees of freedom follow the strata of the design: observations minus estimated means without repeated measures; experimental units minus the treatment combinations they are nested in with repeated measures or subsamples (combination and time when each unit is sampled at a single time); minus one per extra block of each groups column with block structure in the model; and, for groups of units to which some stressors are applied whole (whole plots), the groups minus the combinations of those stressors form their own stratum, which bounds the degrees of freedom of the sets that involve them and is subtracted from those of the other sets. With dispersion = "cell" in fit_responses() the degrees of freedom of each contrast follow the Welch–Satterthwaite approximation (Satterthwaite 1946). Families without a dispersion parameter (Poisson, binomial) and without random effects keep the normal distribution, as in stats::glm(). For Gaussian models without random effects the corrected intervals of AD contrasts are exact t intervals; with repeated measures, and for the interactions between a stressor applied to whole groups and one applied within them, the rule is conservative.

Combinations with only zeros. When the full combination of a set has only zeros at a time (or, for binomial responses, only zeros or only successes) and the model selected by fit_responses() has a log or logit link, the null model still predicts a mean E for it from the other cells. The p-value is twice the probability of observing only zeros if the mean were E, averaged over the draws of E (status = "boundary"; Poisson, NB2, Tweedie, binomial and beta-binomial models). Random intercepts are integrated out: observations that share a level of a random effect share one intercept with the variance of all random terms, which is exact with a single grouping (units or rooms, say) and conservative with nested or crossed ones. The same test is used for a single stressor whose cell has only zeros (against the reference cell). The estimate is computed with the observed mean (zero), which makes MU estimates -Inf; intervals are not given. If the reference cell, or a single-stressor cell that an interaction needs, has only zeros, that contrast cannot be measured and the row is "not_estimable".

Multiple testing. p-values are adjusted within each response, null model, component, stressor and estimand, across contrast sets, sampling times and by groups; averages over times ("overall") are adjusted separately.

Bliss independence

Under Bliss independence ("BL"; Bliss 1939) stressors act independently, so the responses relative to the reference cell, \(w_S = y_S / y_0\) (relative fitness or survival), multiply. Single and combined effects are \(w - 1\), the net interaction is \(w_K - \prod_i w_i\) (the DA measure of Beppler et al. 2016, eqs. 2.1–2.2; Tekin et al. 2018) and, for three stressors, the pure interaction is the emergent interaction E3 of Beppler et al. (2016, eq. 2.4): $$w_{XYZ} - w_X w_{YZ} - w_Y w_{XZ} - w_Z w_{XY} + 2 w_X w_Y w_Z,$$ the part of the three-way deviation that the pairwise interactions do not explain. It is not defined here for four or more stressors (status = "not_defined"). The net BL interaction tests the same hypothesis as the net MU interaction on another scale (a ratio of the combined response to its expectation under MU, a difference under BL); the emergent interaction is a different hypothesis from the pure MU interaction, which removes the pairwise interactions on the log scale.

rescaled divides each BL interaction by the absolute value of the same expression with the combined response replaced by zero, when the interaction is negative (lethal synergy), or by the smallest single-stressor response, when it is positive (complete buffering), so that -1 and 1 mark those two extremes (Segrè et al. 2005; Beppler et al. 2016, section 2.2.3). With a non-negative response it is at least -1; when no stressor increases the response, it exceeds 1 if the combination is less affected than its most affected single stressor. rescaled_class labels values below -0.5 as "synergy", above 0.5 as "antagonism" and the rest as "additive", the conservative cut-offs of Beppler et al. (2016, section 2.2.4). Both describe the size of the interaction only. Whether it deviates from Bliss independence is decided, as for the other null models, by its interval and p-value, because fixed cut-offs ignore the uncertainty of the estimate (Madge Pimentel et al. 2025).

Stress addition and concentration addition

Stress addition (SAM). Liess et al. (2016) assume that each individual tolerates a general stress drawn from a beta distribution with both shape parameters equal to sam_shape. The relative response of each stressor alone, \(w_i\) (survival relative to the reference cell), becomes the general stress whose quantile in that distribution is the mortality \(1 - w_i\); the general stresses of the stressors add up, and the predicted relative response of the combination is the share of individuals that tolerate their sum, zero when it reaches 1 (Liess et al. 2016, eqs. 2-5). The interaction is \(w_K\) minus that prediction; single and combined effects are relative, as under BL. A stressor that increases the response exerts no stress; if one does so at the point estimate, the interaction is "not_applicable". The model predicts larger combined effects than Bliss independence, so combinations that Bliss independence calls additive can be antagonistic under it.

Concentration addition (CA, Loewe additivity). Each stressor acts as a dilution of the others: a combination of doses \(x_i\) has the relative response w at which \(\sum_i x_i / EC_i(w) = 1\), where \(EC_i(w)\) is the dose of stressor i alone that gives w (Loewe 1953; Tang et al. 2015, eq. 2). Doses are the differences between the levels and the control, so the stressor columns must hold numbers. \(EC_i\) comes from a two-parameter log-logistic curve, \(w = 1 / (1 + (x / EC_{50})^b)\), fitted by least squares to the relative responses at every dose of the stressor tested alone, with the other stressors at the reference. At least two such doses are needed, so CA is "not_defined" in two-level factorials. The curves are refitted in each simulation draw, so their uncertainty enters the intervals. A curve that does not decrease with dose makes the interaction "not_applicable"; in single draws it is taken as no dose equivalent. Doses tested alone with only zeros keep their means at the boundary and still inform the curves.

Both models give only the net interaction (the pure interaction of three or more stressors is "not_defined"), and their single and combined effects are those of BL.

Equivalence

A non-significant interaction is a failure to detect a deviation, not evidence of additivity. To claim that a combination follows a null model, declare before the analysis the largest deviation that would be negligible, margin, as a share of the response of the reference cell. Each interaction is then also tested against the hypotheses that its relative deviation d = (observed - expected) / reference is at most -margin and at least margin, with two one-sided tests (Schuirmann 1987; Lakens et al. 2018): p_equivalence is the larger of their p-values.

Each one-sided test measures how far the estimated means of the cells involved are from the closest means at which d equals the bound, in standard errors (the Mahalanobis distance, signed), and compares that distance with a t distribution with the degrees of freedom of the interaction (normal if they are infinite). The distance is measured on a scale on which the variance of a mean does not depend on the mean (Anscombe 1948): the square root for Poisson, quasi-Poisson and other counts whose variance grows in proportion to the mean, the inverse hyperbolic sine of the square root for the negative binomial, the arcsine of the square root for proportions, the logarithm for Gamma and lognormal responses and the response itself for Gaussian ones (for other families, and for models of a transformed response, the scale of the model). When the bounds are linear in the means (AD with a constant variance), the tests are t tests of observed - expected ± margin × reference, as in the t test of a ratio to a control (Hauschke et al. 1999). Tests built from the interval of d, or from its draws, declared false equivalences too often with overdispersed counts, where the standard error of a mean shrinks with the mean. The equivalence test uses neither the draws nor the gradient, so it is the same with both inference methods; near the margin, its verdict can differ from whether the interval of d at 1 - 2 alpha lies within the margin. If the closest means cannot be found, p_equivalence is NA with the note "equivalence_not_tested".

The relative deviation puts every null model on the same scale: under BL, SAM and CA it is the interaction itself; under AD and DO, the interaction divided by the reference; under MU, the observed minus the multiplicative expectation, divided by the reference (the net BL interaction). Its interval includes the uncertainty of the reference. When the stressors raise the response far above the reference (nutrients, say), relative deviations can be large. Combinations with only zeros get a relative deviation but no interval and no test of equivalence.

classify_interactions() and summary() combine both tests, with the adjusted p-values, into four verdicts: "deviation" (deviation detected, not equivalent), "negligible" (a deviation detected, but within the margin), "equivalent" (no deviation detected and within the margin) and "inconclusive" (neither). Only "equivalent" supports a claim that the stressors combine as the null model predicts.

In simulated 2 x 2 experiments with four units per combination, the test declared false equivalence (a true relative deviation exactly at the margin of ±0.25) in 4–6% of the experiments, close to the nominal 5%, for Gaussian responses under AD, survival under BL and overdispersed counts under MU analysed with a quasi-Poisson stats::glm() or with the negative binomial of fit_responses() (3–6% for counts with no, moderate or strong overdispersion). A Poisson model fitted to the same overdispersed counts ignores their overdispersion and gave 21%, which is why fit_responses() uses it only when the negative binomial does not converge; MASS::glm.nb(), whose maximum-likelihood fit with the normal distribution underestimates the variance with so few units, gave 10%. Equivalence needs replication: with four units, a margin of ±0.1 was never reached; one of ±0.25 was reached in about half (Gaussian) to three quarters (survival) of the experiments that followed the null model exactly, but rarely (under 10%) with overdispersed counts.

Default null model

When there is a hypothesis about how the stressors act, name the null model that represents it in null_models (Madge Pimentel et al. 2025); without one, AD is used. It was chosen by simulation, with a rule fixed before the results were seen: among the null models defined in two-level factorials and with at least 80% of the highest average power against interactions that no mechanism explains, the one with the fewest false interactions on average over five mechanisms of no interaction (AD, MU or BL, DO, SAM and CA). The experiments were 2 x 2 factorials and 3 x 3 dose factorials with four units per combination, survival out of 20 animals or overdispersed counts, and moderate or weak single effects, analysed with a cell-means stats::glm() (100 experiments per scenario; p < 0.05 without adjustment).

Each null model flagged interactions at about the nominal rate (3–5%) when the data followed its own mechanism, but none was robust to every mechanism: data generated by stress addition looked synergistic to all the others (in 60% of the experiments under AD, 76% under MU and BL and 86% under DO), and data generated by the others looked antagonistic to stress addition. On average, AD flagged false interactions in 20% of the experiments, MU and BL in 24%, SAM in 27% and DO in 32%, with average powers of 58%, 67%, 38% and 61%. In the dose design CA flagged fewer (16%, against 23% under AD), with less power (51% against 63%). AD was also chosen within each design, each size of the single effects and with survival as the response. Without the stress addition mechanism, MU and BL came within one percentage point of AD and, being more powerful, would have been chosen; with counts only, the power of AD fell below 80% of theirs, and they would have been chosen too. Requiring every null model to agree (agreement = "robust" in compare_null_models()) flagged under 3% false interactions, but only 15% of the interactions that no mechanism explains.

The simulation is installed with the package: system.file("simulations", package = "must") holds the script (null_model_robustness.R), which reruns or extends it, the rates of every scenario (null_model_robustness.csv) and its report (null_model_robustness.md).

Models fitted outside must

Any model supported by emmeans (Lenth & Piaskowski 2026) can be analysed: stats::lm(), stats::glm(), mgcv::gam(), lme4::lmer(), lme4::glmer(), glmmTMB::glmmTMB() and many more. The stressor, time and by columns of design must be predictors of the model; each of their values is a level, also for a numeric predictor, which is evaluated at each value observed. The mean of each treatment combination (and time) is the estimated marginal mean of emmeans: the prediction on the link scale with random effects at zero, averaged with equal weights over the other factors of the model and with other numeric predictors at their mean (unless set in ...), back-transformed with the inverse link or the transformation of the response without bias adjustment (with lm(log(y) ~ ...) they are medians of y, not means). The draws and the delta method use the covariance of the coefficients of the model as it was fitted (no REML refit).

With correction = "small_sample" the degrees of freedom are those emmeans gives for the linear combination of coefficients of each contrast (its gradient for non-linear contrasts): the residual degrees of freedom for stats::lm() and stats::glm() with an estimated dispersion and for mgcv::gam() with any family (observations minus effective degrees of freedom), Kenward–Roger or Satterthwaite for lme4::lmer() when pbkrtest or lmerTest is installed, and infinite for Poisson and binomial models fitted with stats::glm() and for most other mixed models. With few experimental units, infinite degrees of freedom give tests that reject a true null model too often: df sets them by hand, or fit_responses() applies the correction described above.

The estimates inherit the structure of the model. A quantity the model fixes at zero, such as the MU interaction of a log-link model without the interaction term, is "not_applicable". Means the model cannot estimate (in rank-deficient models), or that lie at the boundary of the link function (a combination with only zeros under a log link, or only zeros or only successes under a logit link) make their contrasts "not_estimable": such models give no usable standard error for them, whereas fit_responses() tests them from the probability of that outcome.

Assumptions

  • Means are conditional predictions (random effects at zero). With a log link and a random intercept, marginal means differ by a constant factor: MU and BL estimates and all p-values are unchanged, AD and DO estimates change scale.

  • MU, DO, BL, SAM and CA only represent their mechanistic assumptions when an increase in the response means tolerance (survival, abundance) rather than sensitivity (mortality); declare the latter in sensitivity. AD may predict impossible values below zero, in which case a deviation from it does not imply a mechanistic interaction (Madge Pimentel et al. 2025).

  • A non-significant interaction is a failure to detect a deviation, not evidence of additivity; equivalence needs a margin (see "Equivalence").

Missing values and zeros

MU needs positive means and BL a positive mean in the reference cell: if a fitted or simulated mean is not positive (possible with an identity link), the MU or BL rows of that set are "not_estimable". Treatment combinations without values of the response (at a time) make the sets that need them "not_estimable" (at that time). Times declared as baseline in describe_design() are not estimated.

Reproducibility

With inference = "simulation" results depend on the random number stream: the seed used is in settings$seed, and mc_se gives the Monte Carlo error of each simulated p-value. The same seed may not give identical draws in other versions of R or with other linear algebra libraries.

Examples

jars <- expand.grid(
  salinity = c("ambient", "high"),
  warming = c("no", "yes"),
  replicate = 1:5,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
jars$jar <- seq_len(nrow(jars))
mu <- 40 * ifelse(jars$salinity == "high", 0.5, 1) *
  ifelse(jars$warming == "yes", 0.5, 1)
jars$algae <- stats::qpois(c(0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8)[jars$replicate], mu)
design <- describe_design(jars, c("salinity", "warming"),
  control = c(salinity = "ambient", warming = "no"), unit = "jar")
fits <- fit_responses(jars, "algae", design, residual_checks = FALSE,
  seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
# Simple addition (the default)
est <- estimate_interactions(fits, n_sim = 2000, seed = 1)
est
#> <must_interactions> 1 response(s); null models: AD
#> Inference: Krinsky-Robb simulation (2000 draws), small-sample correction (REML, t); 95% intervals; p-values adjusted with BH; seed 1
#> Scales: AD = differences (response scale)
#> Interactions (1 rows):
#>  response                 combination model estimand estimate lower upper df
#>     algae salinity=high + warming=yes    AD      net      9.8 0.783  19.3 16
#>  p_adj status
#>  0.035     ok
est$estimates[est$estimates$component == "interaction",
  c("null_model", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "df", "p_adjusted")]
#>   null_model estimate    lower    upper df p_adjusted
#> 4         AD      9.8 0.782748 19.30277 16      0.035
# The three null models and the procedure of Madge Pimentel et al. (2025),
# without the correction
estimate_interactions(fits, null_models = c("AD", "MU", "DO"), n_sim = 2000,
  seed = 1, correction = "none")
#> <must_interactions> 1 response(s); null models: AD, MU, DO
#> Inference: Krinsky-Robb simulation (2000 draws), no small-sample correction; 95% intervals; p-values adjusted with BH; seed 1
#> Scales: AD = differences (response scale); MU = log ratios; DO = dominance (response scale)
#> Interactions (3 rows):
#>  response                 combination model estimand  estimate   lower  upper
#>     algae salinity=high + warming=yes    AD      net   9.80000   1.470 18.500
#>     algae salinity=high + warming=yes    MU      net  -0.00501  -0.413  0.413
#>     algae salinity=high + warming=yes    DO      net -10.00000 -12.800 -4.730
#>   df  p_adj status
#>  Inf 0.0160     ok
#>  Inf 0.9700     ok
#>  Inf 0.0005     ok
# Additive, or only not detected? An equivalence margin of 10% of the control
eq <- estimate_interactions(fits, null_models = c("AD", "MU"), n_sim = 2000, seed = 1,
  margin = 0.1)
eq$estimates[eq$estimates$component == "interaction",
  c("null_model", "relative", "relative_lower", "relative_upper", "p_equivalence")]
#>   null_model     relative relative_lower relative_upper p_equivalence
#> 4         AD  0.246231156     0.02237831      0.4369641     0.9145769
#> 8         MU -0.001262594    -0.12707548      0.1096770     0.0560537
classify_interactions(eq)[, c("null_model", "class", "verdict")]
#>   null_model class      verdict
#> 1         AD    -A    deviation
#> 2         MU    AD inconclusive
# Bliss independence, with its rescaled interaction
bl <- estimate_interactions(fits, null_models = "BL", n_sim = 2000, seed = 1)
bl$estimates[bl$estimates$component == "interaction",
  c("estimate", "lower", "upper", "p_value", "rescaled", "rescaled_class")]
#>       estimate      lower    upper p_value rescaled rescaled_class
#> 4 -0.001262594 -0.1270755 0.109677   0.966   -0.005       additive
# A model fitted outside must
model <- stats::glm(algae ~ salinity * warming, family = stats::poisson(), data = jars)
estimate_interactions(model, design, null_models = c("AD", "MU", "BL"), n_sim = 2000,
  seed = 1)
#> <must_interactions> 1 response(s); null models: AD, MU, BL
#> Model: glm, poisson (log); means from emmeans
#> Inference: Krinsky-Robb simulation (2000 draws), degrees of freedom from emmeans; 95% intervals; p-values adjusted with BH; seed 1
#> Scales: AD = differences (response scale); MU = log ratios; BL = relative to the reference cell (Bliss independence)
#> Interactions (3 rows):
#>  response                 combination model estimand estimate  lower   upper
#>     algae salinity=high + warming=yes    AD      net  9.80000  1.470 18.5000
#>     algae salinity=high + warming=yes    MU      net -0.00501 -0.413  0.4130
#>     algae salinity=high + warming=yes    BL      net -0.00126 -0.114  0.0966
#>   df p_adj rescaled status
#>  Inf 0.016       NA     ok
#>  Inf 0.970       NA     ok
#>  Inf 0.970   -0.005     ok
